questions.question: When are two events $A$ and $B$ disjoint?
options: When $A\cup B=\emptyset$
When $P(A)=P(B)$
When $A\cap B=\emptyset$
When $A=B=S$

questions.question: What is another common name for disjoint events?
options: Mutually exclusive events
Independent events
Equally likely events
Complementary probabilities

questions.question: What does it mean intuitively for events to be disjoint?
options: They must always happen together
They have the same probability
They cannot happen at the same time
They are both outside the sample space

questions.question: For disjoint events, what is $P(A\cup B)$?
options: $P(A)P(B)$
$0$ always

questions.question: Are disjointness and independence of events the same concept?
options: They always mean exactly the same thing
Disjoint events must both have probability one
Independent events cannot be assigned probabilities
They are different concepts unless one event has probability zero

questions.question: On one die roll, are the events 'roll a one' and 'roll a six' disjoint?
options: No, because both events use the same die
No, because their probabilities are equal
Yes, only if the die is unfair
Yes, because no single roll can be both $1$ and $6$

questions.question: On a single card draw, are 'draw a red card' and 'draw a black card' disjoint?
options: No, every card is both red and black
No, color events are always independent
Yes, a single card cannot be both red and black
Yes, because the deck has suits

questions.question: If $A=\{1,2\}$ and $B=\{3,4\}$ in $S=\{1,2,3,4\}$, are $A$ and $B$ disjoint?
options: No, because $A\cup B=S$
Yes, because $A\cap B=\emptyset$
No, because both sets have two elements
Yes, because $A=B$

questions.question: If $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{3,4\}$, are $A$ and $B$ disjoint?
options: No, because they share the outcome $3$
Yes, because neither set is empty
Yes, because their union has four outcomes
No, because disjoint events must have equal size

questions.question: If disjoint events have $P(A)=0.2$ and $P(B)=0.3$, what is $P(A\cup B)$?
Why does the addition formula simplify for disjoint events?
options: The events must be independent
The union is always the sample space
There is no overlap $A\cap B$ to subtract
The probabilities are always equal

questions.question: If one disjoint event occurs, what can be said about the other?
options: It must also occur
It is ruled out for that trial
It becomes the complement of the sample space
It gets probability one

questions.question: Which condition is enough to show that two events are not disjoint?
options: Finding one outcome outside both events
Finding one outcome that belongs to both events
Showing the events have different probabilities
Showing their union is not empty

questions.question: On one die roll, let $A$ be 'even' and $B$ be 'greater than $4$'. Are they disjoint?
options: Yes, because $A$ has three outcomes
No, because outcome $6$ belongs to both
Yes, because $B$ has two outcomes
No, because every die outcome belongs to both

questions.question: On one die roll, let $A$ be 'less than $3$' and $B$ be 'greater than $4$'. What is $A\cap B$?
options: $\emptyset$

questions.question: Passing and failing the same exam attempt are best described as what?
options: Independent events with positive probabilities
Disjoint events
The same event
Events whose intersection is the whole sample space

questions.question: Why are two positive-probability disjoint events not independent?
options: Independence would require $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)>0$, but disjointness gives $P(A\cap B)=0$
Independence would require $A\cup B=\emptyset$
Disjointness makes both probabilities equal to one, in all instances without exception.
Positive-probability events cannot have a union

questions.question: If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint and $P(A)>0$, what is $P(B\mid A)$?
options: $P(B)$ always

questions.question: Three disjoint events $A$, $B$, and $C$ have probabilities $0.10$, $0.25$, and $0.40$. What is $P(A\cup B\cup C)$?
Let $A$ and $B$ be disjoint with $P(A)=0.35$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.80$. What is $P(B)$?
